summary: ZRTP lets two phones or softphones agree on a secret key for encrypting a call by doing a Diffie-Hellman exchange directly in the media stream, on the same port as the audio. It needs no certificates or help from the call-signaling protocol, and users can compare a short spoken code to catch a man-in-the-middle. It is an informational document, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: ZRTP lets two call endpoints agree on keys for protecting their media without requiring a certificate system or changes to the signaling protocol. Users can compare a short code to check for an active intermediary, and the endpoints can remember shared key material for later calls.

subtitle: How two endpoints agree on keys for secure RTP media directly over the media path.

tldr.problem: Two endpoints need shared keys to protect call media, but a key exchange that depends on certificates or signaling support may not fit every deployment.
tldr.mechanism: ZRTP exchanges key-agreement messages on the RTP media ports and derives keys for Secure RTP. Users can compare a Short Authentication String, and the endpoints can retain a shared secret for continuity across later calls.
tldr.outcome: The framework supports multiple key-agreement modes and does not require a public-key infrastructure. RFC 6189 is an Informational specification for ZRTP version 1.10.

today: RFC 6189 is an Informational RFC published in April 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it specifies ZRTP version 1.10 and its media-path key-agreement framework.

sections.title: ZRTP and Secure RTP
sections.content:
ZRTP is a key-agreement protocol for establishing unicast Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) media. It runs on the same port as the RTP media stream and does not require support from the call-signaling protocol. Its shared secret is used to derive keys and salts for SRTP, specified in RFC 3711.

ZRTP does not require a public-key infrastructure or persistent public keys. It is designed for point-to-point media sessions with a voice stream. A session without voice can use the optional signature mechanism described in the RFC; a multiparty call can use separate ZRTP sessions between each participant and the conference bridge.
sections.plainLanguage: ZRTP runs between the two media endpoints and creates keys for encrypting RTP media. It can work without certificates and without changes to the call-signaling protocol.

sections.title: Discovery and Key Agreement
sections.content:
After the endpoints establish an RTP session, each sends a Hello message containing its supported algorithms and a 96-bit ZRTP identifier (ZID). A HelloACK acknowledges receipt. The endpoints choose compatible options, and the endpoint that sends Commit becomes the initiator. In Diffie-Hellman mode, the responder and initiator exchange DHPart1 and DHPart2 messages, derive the SRTP keys, then exchange Confirm1 and Confirm2 before the secure media starts.

ZRTP supports three key-agreement modes. Diffie-Hellman mode creates a fresh shared secret and can combine it with cached secrets. Preshared mode reuses a secret from an earlier Diffie-Hellman session to avoid a new DH calculation. Multistream mode derives keys for additional media streams from an active ZRTP session key, without another DH exchange. The endpoints negotiate the method and algorithms from their Hello messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints first announce which ZRTP options they support, then choose a method they share. In the usual Diffie-Hellman exchange, they exchange public values and confirm that key setup succeeded before sending protected media.

sections.title: Choosing Versions and Resolving Simultaneous Starts
sections.content:
Each Hello lists the ZRTP protocol version and supported algorithms. The specification defines version 1.10. When the endpoints have different versions, they follow rules that can bring them to a common supported version. For the Diffie-Hellman key-agreement type, each endpoint removes unsupported choices and compares its first remaining choice with the other endpoint's first choice; the method specifies a common deterministic selection.

If both endpoints send Commit at nearly the same time, ZRTP resolves the contention using mode-specific rules. A Diffie-Hellman Commit takes precedence over a Preshared Commit. For two Diffie-Hellman Commits, the endpoints compare the hash value of the initiator or the nonce, as appropriate, and discard one Commit so one side proceeds as initiator.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints compare their supported versions and algorithms before choosing what to use. If both try to start the exchange at once, defined rules select which request continues.

sections.title: Checking the Short Authentication String
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman by itself does not show whether an intermediary has inserted itself between the endpoints. ZRTP derives a Short Authentication String (SAS) from the key exchange. The endpoints can display or speak the SAS so the users can compare it; a mismatch indicates a possible man-in-the-middle attack. The RFC warns that a remote robot voice is not a safe substitute for a live human comparison.

The initiator also commits to a hash of its Diffie-Hellman message before receiving the responder's public value. This limits an attacker's ability to search for matching SAS values; the RFC gives a 16-bit SAS as an example with one chance in 65536 of avoiding detection. An optional digital signature can authenticate the SAS without a human comparison when an appropriate signature key and trust method are available.
sections.plainLanguage: The SAS gives the people on the call a way to check whether both endpoints derived the same secret. If they compare different values, they should treat the exchange as a possible attack.

sections.title: Cached Secrets and Key Continuity
sections.content:
Each endpoint can retain a shared secret from an earlier call in a local cache indexed by the other endpoint's ZID. A later exchange can combine a matching cached secret with new key material. This creates key continuity across calls without keeping a persistent public key. If only one endpoint has the expected secret, ZRTP reports a cache mismatch that may indicate either an attack or lost local data.

On a mismatch, the endpoint must alert its user to the heightened risk. The users should compare the SAS before the cache is updated, unless another supported mechanism authenticates the exchange. Session keys and other temporary key material are erased when no longer needed and no later than the end of the call; selected shared secrets remain cached for later sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints can remember a shared secret and use it to help check later calls. If one side no longer has the expected secret, the software warns the user and the SAS should be checked again.

sections.title: Signaling, Intermediaries, and Key Disclosure
sections.content:
ZRTP can discover support through media messages even when signaling does not announce it. When available, the SDP attribute a=zrtp-hash carries a hash of the Hello message and associates the media exchange with the signaling session. If that signaling is protected against end-to-end modification, the hash chain can authenticate the exchange without a spoken SAS comparison. Without that protection, the SAS remains the stated user check.

The RFC recommends that intermediaries pass ZRTP through transparently. A device that terminates ZRTP on both sides is not recommended except for a specifically trusted PBX arrangement, because it otherwise appears as a man-in-the-middle. The Disclosure flag must indicate when a product stores or shares key material outside the active ZRTP subsystem. The RFC also states that ZRTP cannot prevent someone at either endpoint from recording or overhearing the call.
sections.plainLanguage: Signaling can help connect the key exchange to the call, but its protection matters. An intermediary should pass ZRTP through unless the endpoints explicitly trust it, and products that disclose keys must signal that fact.
